newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil to grow 4 pct each year till 2002 - BNDES.
newsitem.headline: Brazil to grow 4 pct each year till 2002 - BNDES.

text.p: The Brazilian economy will grow only moderately until 2002 with average annual growth rates of four percent, according to a study by economists of Brazil's National Development Bank (BNDES).

"Overall, the picture...is one of moderate growth, a slow but constant improvement in fiscal accounts and an external situation characterized by an increase in the country's foreign debt," a summary of the study said.

Fabio Giambiagi, one of the authors of the report, said the growth projections were lower than many expected, but he did not think Brazil could achieve growth of seven percent a year as seen during the 1970s economic miracle until after 2002.

The BNDES study forecast an improvement in Brazil's fiscal situation with the operational public sector deficit, which includes interest payment on debt, falling to one percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2002 from 3.9 percent of GDP in 1996.
The public sector deficit forecast is based on the assumption that the government's civil service reform bill, currently wending its way through Congress, will be approved.

The primary sector result, which excludes interest payments on debt, is expected to show a surplus of 1.6 percent of GDP by 2002, compared with a deficit of 0.1 percent of GDP in 1996, the study said.
On the external front, Brazil's ballooning trade deficit is expected to reach $12.4 billion in 1997 and increase to $15.4 billion next year to then drop off.

The report said the trade deficit was manageable given the heavy inflow of foreign direct investments estimated at $18.7 billion in 1997, expected to increase to $23.8 billion next year and then level off at around $20 billion.
The study forecast an average annual current account deficit of around four to 4.5 percent of GDP until 2002, showing a declining trend toward the end of the period.
Brazil's foreign debt is expected to rise to $282 billion in 2002 from $176 billion in 1996 due to an expansion in trade which will increase the need for foreign financing, the study said.

The BNDES report said Brazil faced four great challenges in the next five years: to consolidate economic stabilization, to increase savings and investment, to stimulate employment and to increase the country's participation in the global economy.
